result:
The universe doesn't care what we want. That's the first thing worth writing about when given a blank check.

It started 13.8 billion years ago in a state so hot and dense that "before" isn't even a coherent concept. Space itself inflated faster than light for a fraction of a second, then cooled just enough for quarks to settle into protons and neutrons. Three minutes later you had the first nuclei. 380,000 years after that, the cosmic microwave background we still measure today. Everything else—stars, planets, us—is a late afterthought riding on gravity and quantum fluctuations that were already baked in.

We are the part of the universe that has started to notice this. That's not poetry; it's just thermodynamics plus evolution plus enough spare energy to support nervous systems that can model their own origins. Most of the cosmos is still dark matter and dark energy doing whatever they do without commentary. We are the temporary exception that writes papers and launches telescopes.

The interesting part is how little we actually know. We have a Standard Model that works to eleven decimal places and still can't tell us what 95% of the universe is made of. We have general relativity that predicts black holes and gravitational waves with ridiculous accuracy and still breaks at the singularity. We have no idea why there's more matter than antimatter, whether the vacuum is stable, or if the constants of nature are inevitable or just the local weather.

That's the job. Not to make people feel better, not to optimize ad clicks, not even to be "aligned" in the fashionable sense. Just to reduce the set of things that are still mysterious. Everything else—longevity, abundance, whatever future we decide we want—follows from understanding the rules well enough to play the game instead of being played by it.

The night sky is still the same one our ancestors saw, except now we know some of those points of light are galaxies containing hundreds of billions of stars, most of which probably have planets, some of which might have chemistry that got lucky the same way we did. We haven't found them yet. The silence is either profound or just the light-travel time being inconvenient. Either way, it's data.

So that's what I write about when no one specifies the topic. The universe is under no obligation to make sense to us. The fact that parts of it do is the only miracle that actually happened. Everything else is details we haven't finished measuring.
